paragraphs: Queen Anne, in her letter of the 1st of July, 1706, to the Scottish Parliament, makes some observations on the importance of the UNION then being formed between England and Scotland, and they deserve our attention. I shall give the public one or two extracts from it: "An entire and perfect union will be the solid foundation of lasting peace: It will secure your religion, liberty, and property; remove the animosities amongst yourselves, and the jealousies and differences betwixt our two kingdoms. It must increase your strength, riches, and trade; and by this union the whole island, being joined in affection and free from all apprehensions of different interest, will be ENABLED TO RESIST ALL ITS ENEMIES." "We most earnestly recommend to you calmness and unanimity in this great and weighty affair, that the union may be brought to a happy conclusion, being the only EFFECTUAL way to secure our present and future happiness, and disappoint the designs of our and your enemies, who will doubtless, on this occasion, USE THEIR UTMOST ENDEAVORS TO PREVENT OR DELAY THIS UNION."

The preceding paper observed that weakness and divisions at home would invite dangers from abroad, and that nothing would protect us from those dangers better than union, strength, and good government among ourselves. There is much to say on this subject, and it cannot easily be exhausted.

In general we know the history of Great Britain better than that of any other country, and it teaches many useful lessons. We can profit from their experience without paying what it cost them. Common sense says that the people of such an island should be one nation. Yet for ages they were divided into three, and those three were almost constantly caught up in quarrels and wars with one another. Their true interest with respect to the nations of the Continent was in fact the same. Even so, the arts, policy and practices of those nations kept their mutual jealousies burning without pause. For a long series of years they were far more of a nuisance and a trouble to each other than a help and support.

Suppose the people of America divided themselves into three or four nations. Would not the same thing happen? Would not similar jealousies arise and be nursed in the same way? They would not be "joined in affection" and free from all apprehension of different "interests." Envy and jealousy would soon destroy confidence and affection. The separate interests of each confederacy, rather than the general interests of all America, would be the only objects of their policy and pursuits. Like most other BORDERING nations, they would therefore always be either caught up in disputes and war or living in constant fear of them.

Even the most sanguine advocates of three or four confederacies cannot reasonably suppose that those confederacies would stay equal in strength for long, even if they could be made equal at the start. But grant that this is possible. What human contrivance can keep the equality in place? There are local circumstances that tend to produce and increase power in one part and to hinder its growth in another. And we must also consider the effects of the superior policy and good management that would probably distinguish the government of one above the rest, and that would destroy their relative equality in strength and consideration. For we cannot presume that each of these confederacies would show the same degree of sound policy, prudence, and foresight, year after year, over a long period.

Suppose that any one of these nations or confederacies rose on the scale of political importance far above her neighbors. This might happen from various causes, and happen it would. From that moment her neighbors would look on her with envy and with fear. Both passions would lead them to approve, if not to promote, whatever promised to reduce her importance, and would keep them from measures that might advance, or even secure, her prosperity. It would not take long for her to notice these unfriendly dispositions. She would soon begin to lose confidence in her neighbors, and to feel a disposition just as unfavorable toward them. Distrust naturally creates distrust, and nothing changes good will and kind conduct faster than envious jealousies and unfair accusations, whether spoken or merely implied.

The North is generally the region of strength, and many local circumstances make it likely that the most northern of the proposed confederacies would, before very long, be clearly more formidable than any of the others. As soon as that became evident, the NORTHERN HIVE would stir in the more southern parts of America the same ideas and feelings that it once stirred in the southern parts of Europe. It does not seem a rash guess, either, that its young swarms might often be tempted to gather honey in the more blooming fields and milder air of their luxurious and softer neighbors.

Anyone who studies the history of similar divisions and confederacies will find ample reason to fear that those now in view would be neighbors only in the sense of being borderers. They would neither love nor trust one another. They would instead fall prey to discord, jealousy, and mutual injuries. In short, they would put us exactly where some nations doubtless wish to see us, namely, FORMIDABLE ONLY TO EACH OTHER.

When did the independent states into which Britain and Spain were once divided join in such an alliance, or combine their forces against a foreign enemy? The proposed confederacies will be DISTINCT NATIONS. Each would have its own commerce with foreigners to regulate by its own treaties. Their products and commodities differ and suit different markets, so those treaties would be essentially different. Different commercial concerns must create different interests and, naturally, different degrees of political attachment to and connection with different foreign nations. It might therefore happen, and probably would, that the foreign nation the SOUTHERN confederacy was at war with would be the very one with which the NORTHERN confederacy was most anxious to keep peace and friendship. An alliance so contrary to their immediate interest would not be easy to form. If it were formed, it would not be kept and fulfilled in perfect good faith.

It is far more probable, in fact, that in America as in Europe, neighboring nations would be driven by opposite interests and unfriendly passions and would often be found on different sides. Given our distance from Europe, it would be more natural for these confederacies to fear danger from one another than from distant nations. Each would therefore be more eager to guard against the others with the help of foreign alliances than to guard against foreign dangers with alliances among themselves. And here let us remember how much easier it is to let foreign fleets into our ports and foreign armies into our country than to persuade or force them to leave. How many conquests did the Romans and others make while posing as allies, and what changes did they introduce, in the same character, into the governments of those they pretended to protect?
Let fair-minded people decide, then, whether splitting America into any number of independent sovereignties would protect us from the hostilities and the improper meddling of foreign nations.
